svg.text: SAMPLING — WHO GETS LEFT OUT DECIDES WHAT YOU FIND
A sample is not a small copy of the population unless you took the trouble to make it one.

g.text: Simple random — every person equally likely
Systematic — every tenth name on the list
Stratified — divide by ward or region first,
then sample within each, keeping proportions
Cluster — sample whole villages or wards

svg.text: Can generalise. Needs a list of the population.

g.text: Convenience — whoever is on the ward today
Purposive — chosen because they know about it
Snowball — one participant introduces the next,
used for hidden or stigmatised groups
Quota — fill fixed numbers in each category

svg.text: Cheap and quick. Cannot claim to represent.
SELECTION BIAS IS BUILT IN BEFORE ANY DATA IS COLLECTED

g.text: Survey satisfaction only in the outpatient queue and you have already excluded everyone too ill to come,
everyone who could not afford the transport, and everyone so dissatisfied that they stopped attending.
No amount of statistics later can repair a sample that never contained the people who mattered.

svg.text: BIGGER IS NOT THE SAME AS BETTER

g.text: Two thousand people from one clinic
still describe only that one clinic.

svg.text: IN QUALITATIVE WORK, STOP AT SATURATION

g.text: When new interviews add no new theme,
the sample is finished. It may be twelve.

svg.text: Always ask who is missing from this sample, and whether they differ in the very thing being measured.
